headline: Monhegan ledges on the ebb: pollock topside, cod deep, bass stacking the rivers
subhead: Cold water's holding the bay quiet, but the river mouths and Monhegan's ledges are still giving up fish for those who know where to look.
body_markdown:
Forty-one years hauling gear and chasing fish out of this harbor, and I can tell you the second week of August has a rhythm that doesn't change much, even when everything else does. I was out hauling off Two Bush Island Tuesday morning when Dave Alley came over the radio griping that Eastern Egg Rock was thick with mackerel and not a tern working them. That told me more than any thermometer could. When the bait's that dense and the birds aren't diving, it means the mackerel are holding deep and steady, not getting pushed around by anything chasing them hard. That's been the story of this whole stretch of water for weeks now — steady, cold, and unbothered.

We called this one last week — said Midcoast Maine would stay the calmest, coldest zone on the chart, and here we are. Nothing's shifted. The Gulf of Maine water sitting on Penobscot Bay hasn't warmed a lick, and that cold cushion is keeping the southern fish — the bluefish especially — mostly out of the picture this far north. I've had exactly one report of a bluefish this month, a single fish off Ram Island, and I wouldn't build a trip around them right now. If you want blues, you're better off waiting till Labor Day, if they show at all.

What's working is what always works when the bay stays cold: striped bass holding tight to the river mouths where the water warms up and the bait concentrates. The Damariscotta River mouth, down around the Gut and the flats off Fort Island, has been giving up bass to 30 inches on the last two hours of the outgoing tide. Sea worms fished on a simple slip rig, or chunked mackerel drifted along the current seam where the river water meets the salt, has been the ticket. The Medomak River mouth off Waldoboro has been similar — smaller fish mostly, schoolies in the 18 to 24 inch range, but they're stacked thick enough on the outgoing that a bucktail or a swimming plug worked slow along bottom will connect more often than not. The Back River up behind Southport has had a few slot fish too, taken on topwater at first light before the sun gets on the water — Zara Spooks and pencil poppers worked over the mussel flats on the last of the flood.

Monhegan's been the bright spot for anybody willing to make the run. Pollock have been busting bait on the surface off White Head and around the ledges to the northeast of the harbor, especially in the last hour of the ebb when the current pulls hard around the island and pushes bait up against the rock. Diamond jigs, 2 to 4 ounces depending on the drift, worked with a fast retrieve through the boils — that's been about as reliable a bite as we've had all summer. Fish are running 3 to 6 pounds, with the occasional bigger one mixed in. If you see the surface nervous with bait and gulls dropping in, that's your window, and it doesn't stay open long — twenty, thirty minutes before the current slacks and the fish drop back down.

Groundfish are still where they've been all season — deep, and patient anglers are still finding them. Cod are holding in the channels around Isle au Haut Bay and off the eastern side of Vinalhaven, 140 to 180 feet, on the last of the ebb when the current's still moving enough to keep bait suspended off bottom. Haddock have been scarcer this far into the bay — you'll do better running out toward Matinicus if haddock specifically is the target, but a few have come up mixed in with the cod on jigs worked right off the bottom, three or four cranks up and let it settle again. Nothing's been fast, but it's been steady, and for August in a bay this cold, steady is about what you can ask for.

The moon's building toward new on the 12th, and that's the one thing I'd watch closest over the next several days. More tidal range means more current, and more current at spots like the Muscle Ridge Channel, the mouth of the Damariscotta, and around Monhegan's ledges usually sharpens things up rather than shutting them down. If the extra push gets the bait moving more aggressively, I'd expect the pollock bite at Monhegan to hold or improve, and I'd expect the river-mouth bass to feed a little harder on that stronger outgoing water. I wouldn't count on the bluefish showing just because the tide's building — that's a water temperature problem, not a current problem, and nothing in the pattern suggests that's changing soon. My money this week is on the same three spots that have been paying off: the Damariscotta mouth on the outgoing, Monhegan's ledges on the last of the ebb, and the deep channels around Isle au Haut for anybody patient enough to soak a jig.
